fields.label: Appliances that run at the same time
fields.hint: Pick each appliance, check the watts against its label, and set how many hours a day it runs. Add every load that can be on at once.

fields.name: sanctioned_kw
fields.label: Sanctioned load
fields.hint: The kW printed on your electricity bill; it sets the fixed charge in the bill estimate. Blank uses {{d.default_sanctioned_kw|int}} kW. At {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} kW or more the bill is on a ToU meter: use the [[F13|ToU bill calculator]].

fields.name: pf
fields.label: Power factor
fields.hint: Leave blank to use each appliance's own power factor: heaters, irons, kettles and geysers 1.0, inverter ACs 0.9, motors and compressors about 0.8. A figure here is used for every row.

outputs.label: Peak with the largest motor starting

answer: A typical home with {{out.items|int}} appliances running together (fans, lights, a fridge, a TV, a 1.5 ton inverter AC and a water pump) draws about {{out.running_w|int}} W, or {{out.amps|1}} A at {{out.volts|int}} V, and uses about {{out.monthly_units|int}} units a month. Add your own appliances below to get your total watts, peak load, amps and monthly units.
how: Running load = the watts of every appliance × its quantity, added up = {{out.running_w|int}} W. Peak load adds the starting surge of the largest motor = {{out.peak_w|int}} W. Current = {{out.running_w|int}} W ÷ ({{out.volts}} V × {{out.pf|2}} power factor) = {{out.amps|1}} A. Energy = each appliance's watts × hours a day (an inverter AC counts at its average draw, below its rated watts), added up = {{out.daily_kwh|1}} units a day, × {{out.days|2}} days = {{out.monthly_units|int}} units a month. Bill: {{out.monthly_units|int}} units reach the {{out.bill_rate|rs2}} slab, so every unit is charged at that rate = {{out.bill_energy_rs|rs}}, plus the fixed charge for {{out.bill_kw|int}} kW, FC surcharge, QTA and GST (no FPA, unprotected) = {{out.monthly_rs|rs}} a month, the same as the electricity bill calculator gives for these units.
key_facts: Home electrical load in watts = the sum of the running watts of every appliance that is on at the same time; divide by volts × power factor to get amps.
Peak load adds the starting surge of the largest motor or compressor only once, because two motors rarely start in the same instant.
Monthly units (kWh) = watts × hours a day ÷ 1,000 × {{d.days_per_month|2}} days, added over every appliance; this is the number your electricity bill is based on.

The default example home above ({{out.items|int}} appliances of {{out.appliances|int}} kinds) draws {{out.running_w|int}} W running, {{out.peak_w|int}} W at peak and uses about {{out.monthly_units|int}} units a month.

formula.text: P = Σ (W × qty); I = P ÷ (V × PF); units/day = Σ (W × qty × h) ÷ 1000
lines: P = total running load in watts
W = running watts of one appliance, qty = how many
I = current in amps, V = supply voltage, PF = power factor
h = hours a day the appliance runs
Peak = P + the largest (starting watts − running watts) of any motor

sections.h2: Running load, peak load and monthly units: what each number is for
p: The {{out.running_w|int}} W running load of the default home is what an inverter, UPS or generator must carry for as long as everything is on, and what the main breaker sees. The {{out.peak_w|int}} W peak is the moment the largest motor or compressor starts on top of that load: it sets the surge rating of an inverter and, more often than the running load, the size of a generator.

The {{out.monthly_units|int}} units a month are a different quantity: energy, not power. They are what the bill charges for and what a solar system has to produce. Take the running and peak watts to the [[D4|inverter size calculator]] or the [[C1|generator size calculator]], and the daily units to the [[D7|solar system size calculator]].

The sanctioned load printed on the bill is the kW the DISCO agreed to supply to the house. Enter it and this calculator compares the running load with it: the third worked example, with a non-inverter AC and a geyser, runs at {{ex.2.out.load_pct|int}}% of a {{ex.2.out.sanctioned_kw|int}} kW sanctioned load. A running load close to or above the sanctioned load is the usual reason a home is told to apply for a load extension before adding an AC or solar.

Not everything in a house runs at once, so the sanctioned load to apply for is worked out from the connected load with a diversity factor. The [[N4|sanctioned load calculator]] does that, and the [[E4|load check before adding an AC]] shows whether one more AC fits the connection you have.

sections.h2: Home load in amps and the wiring
p: At {{out.volts|int}} V and a power factor of {{d.pf_mixed|2}}, the default running load of {{out.running_w|int}} W is {{out.amps|1}} A on a single-phase supply. That is the current the main cable and the main breaker carry when everything on the list is running.

Each circuit in the house carries only its own share, so wire and breaker sizes are chosen circuit by circuit. Use the [[N18|home wiring load schedule]] to size every circuit at once, or the [[W3|MCB size calculator]] for one circuit; have a licensed electrician confirm the main breaker and cable before changing them.

examples.title: Small home: {{out.appliances|int}} kinds of appliance, no AC
examples.text: Three fans, eight LED bulbs, a TV and a fridge total {{out.running_w|int}} W running and {{out.peak_w|int}} W when the fridge compressor starts, which is {{out.amps|1}} A at {{out.volts|int}} V. They use about {{out.daily_kwh|1}} units a day and {{out.monthly_units|int}} units a month, within a {{out.sanctioned_kw|int}} kW sanctioned load.

examples.title: Family home with two inverter ACs
examples.text: Five fans, twelve bulbs, a fridge, two 1.5 ton inverter ACs, an iron and a water pump come to {{out.running_w|int}} W running and {{out.peak_w|int}} W at peak, or {{out.amps|1}} A. Expect about {{out.monthly_units|int}} units a month, an estimated bill of {{out.monthly_rs|rs}} at the {{out.bill_rate|rs2}} slab, using {{out.load_pct|int}}% of a {{out.sanctioned_kw|int}} kW sanctioned load.

examples.title: Non-inverter AC plus an electric geyser on a {{out.sanctioned_kw|int}} kW connection
examples.text: The running load is {{out.running_w|int}} W, but the non-inverter compressor pushes the peak to {{out.peak_w|int}} W, or {{out.peak_amps|1}} A for a moment. At {{out.load_pct|int}}% of the sanctioned load this connection is overloaded; a higher sanctioned load or an inverter AC is the fix.

mistakes: Adding every appliance in the house. Only count what runs at the same time; an iron used for half an hour matters for the monthly units but rarely for the peak load.

Using the AC's rated input as its average draw. An inverter AC's input varies with the room temperature; the watts here are a planning average, and the rated maximum is used for wire and breaker sizing.
Ignoring starting surge. A non-inverter AC or a water pump draws about three times its running watts for a second or two, which is what trips an undersized breaker or inverter.
Confusing watts with units. Watts are the rate of use right now; units (kWh) are watts × hours ÷ 1,000 and are what the bill charges for.
safety: If the running load is close to your sanctioned load or your main breaker rating, do not add more; ask your DISCO for a higher sanctioned load and have a licensed electrician check the main cable and breaker.

faq.q: How do I calculate the electrical load of my house?
faq.a: List every appliance that can run at the same time, take the running watts from its label or the [[H2|appliance list]], multiply by how many you have and add them up. Divide the total by volts × power factor ({{d.v_1ph|int}} V × {{d.pf_mixed|2}} in Pakistan) for amps.

faq.q: What is the total load of a house in kW?
faq.a: Most Pakistani homes without an AC run at well under one kilowatt; a home with one inverter AC, fans, lights and a fridge runs at about {{out.running_kw|1}} kW, and each extra inverter AC adds about {{d.ac_inverter_avg_kw_1_5_ton|1}} kW on average and more at full speed.

faq.q: What is a connected load and how is it different from running load?
faq.a: Connected load is the sum of everything wired in the house; running load is what is on at the same moment. Bills and sanctioned loads are set against expected demand, so the running load is the number to plan with.

faq.q: How many units does this load use per month?
faq.a: Each appliance's watts × hours a day ÷ 1,000 gives its units a day; add them and multiply by {{d.days_per_month|2}}. The default home above uses about {{out.daily_kwh|1}} units a day and {{out.monthly_units|int}} a month.

faq.q: Can I use this load to size a UPS, inverter or solar system?
faq.a: Yes. The running watts are the continuous rating your inverter or UPS needs (plus a safety margin), the peak watts are its surge rating, and the daily units are what a solar system must produce. The next-step links below take your numbers to those calculators.

faq.q: What is the electrical load estimation for a new house?
faq.a: Add the rooms' lights and fans, one AC per bedroom you plan to cool, the kitchen appliances and the water pump, then apply a diversity factor because not everything runs together; the sanctioned-load calculator does this and recommends the kW to apply for.
